newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Europe's gas bubble may burst by 2005, experts say.
newsitem.headline: Europe's gas bubble may burst by 2005, experts say.

text.p: Natural gas production is lagging way behind soaring demand in Europe and consumers may face shortages early next decade if new suppliers do not enter the market, industry officials meeting in Geneva said on Friday.

Officials from producer nations including Russia, Britain and Norway, in a statement at the end of this week's meeting, said European gas demand was at an all-time high and forecast to rise by 50 percent by 2010.
But output, already declining in some countries but seen as generally stable for now, was expected to decrease after 2005.

"Production in several European countries is already down, and after 2005 there'll be an overall decrease, giving rise to a serious supply gap," said Yves Berthelot, executive secretary of the United Nations' economic cooperation agency for Europe, the Economic Commission for Europe (ECE) which chaired the talks.
Total gas consumption soared to 1.02 trillion cubic metres in 1995 from 320 billion in 1970 in western, central and eastern Europe and Russia and the former Soviet republics, ECE said.
It gave no output data in comparison but said the industry estimated the supply gap by 2010 at 90 billion cubic metres.
Executive vice-president of Norway's Statoil, Peter Mellbye, told the meeting that Norway's exports were expected to more than double to 65 billion cubic metres a year after 2000.
Britain also had enough gas reserves to cover both domestic demand and exports up to 2005, according to Peter Jessen, head of European marketing at British Gas.
But meeting long-term supply needs would be a major challenge, the officials said.

New suppliers expected to enter the market such as Nigeria and South American producers and higher output from Iran should provide some relief, but mobilising distant gas reserves and guaranteeing security of supplies would be very costly.

ECE said new supplies in remote areas of the North Sea and Barents Sea, Russia -- the Yamal peninsula in particular, the southern Sahara in Algeria, the Middle East, the Gulf of Guinea and from Central and Latin America required new transmission infrastructures and billions of dollars in investment.
